findings: Hazan's OCO protocol is sequential: choose x_t, then observe f_t; it assumes bounded losses/cost functions and a bounded or structured decision set. The plan distinguishes full-information and bandit feedback and distinguishes oblivious, past-adaptive non-anticipating, current-action-reactive and stochastic environments so that guarantees cannot silently cross adversary models.

Static regret, realized regret, expected regret, stochastic finite-arm pseudo-regret, dynamic regret, and interval/adaptive regret are given separately. Pseudo-regret is tied to the conditional-mean stochastic arm model, where its expectation agrees with expected realized reward regret.

Hazan defines dynamic regret against a comparator sequence and path length P(u_1:T)=1+sum_{t=1}^{T-1}||u_t-u_{t+1}||. Adaptive regret is the maximum interval regret. Strong adaptivity is described as a per-interval comparison to a specified base algorithm up to explicit polylog(T) factors. The source's FLH/FLH2 proof details deferred to exercises are not imported, and no anytime confidence or statistical-validity claim is inferred.

findings: Hazan Theorem 1.5 gives Hedge's expected loss against any fixed expert for nonnegative full-information losses: the bound includes epsilon times the algorithm-distribution-weighted sum of squared losses plus log(N)/epsilon. For losses in [0,1], the squared-loss term is at most T, yielding the stated 2sqrt(T log N) tuning; no full-information adversarial-loss bound is transferred to bandit feedback.

Hazan Theorem 3.1 and displayed proof use Euclidean projected OGD, D=diam(K), gradient bound G, and step size eta_t=D/(G sqrt(t)), giving regret at most (3/2)DG sqrt(T). Its proof is for differentiable convex costs. The plan's subgradient variant is expressly local and assumes a selected subgradient satisfying the inequality against all comparators in K.

The library suppliers match the required first-order and projection interfaces. The Hilbert projection existence theorem assumes Countable Choice; the plan carries that premise. Hazan's minimax lower-bound derivation is left as an exercise and is not claimed.

findings: Hazan Definition 5.1 defines the asymmetric Bregman divergence, and Algorithm 14's agile OMD update plus Theorem 5.6 give the exact coefficient eta/4 on the local dual-Hessian norm sum and (R(u)-R(x_1))/(2 eta). The theorem's tuned D_R G_R sqrt(T) consequence follows under the bounded regularizer diameter and local-gradient bounds.

Theorem 5.6 proof uses convexity, the Bregman three-point identity, the Bregman projection Pythagorean inequality, the local Hessian dual norm, nonnegativity and telescoping. These arguments are retained as local proof obligations; no published Bregman/OMD item was found.

The Euclidean regularizer recovers projected OGD by direct algebra. Negative entropy recovers the normalized multiplicative update on the positive simplex, while its entropy-diameter and projection-normalization derivations are exercises and remain local obligations.

AdaGrad Algorithm 19 uses cumulative gradient Gram matrices and Moore–Penrose inverse updates. The source's printed diagonal scale reads diag(G_t^(1/2)); the coordinatewise diagonal update is stated in the scaffold only with an explicit local notation/proof obligation. Theorem 5.12 relies on Proposition 5.16, whose optimizer proof is an exercise, so no AdaGrad rate is claimed.

findings: Lattimore–Szepesvári define the stochastic finite-arm environment through arm reward laws and history-conditional action/reward kernels. Finite means and an attained optimal arm support the gap, pseudo-regret and expected-regret decomposition.

Theorem 6.1 gives the stated explore-then-commit expected-regret bound for 1-subgaussian arms and 1<=m<=n/k. The book leaves the exact 2/m-subgaussian difference proof to Exercise 6.1 and relies on its Chapter 5 independent-sum lemma, whose proof is Exercise 5.7; the plan supplies a local MGF/product-law/Tonelli/Markov proof obligation.

Theorem 7.1 and Theorem 7.2 give the stated UCB expected gap-dependent and gap-free bounds for delta=1/n^2. The proof replaces random pull counts with independent reward-table prefixes and a finite union bound, so the scaffold explicitly forbids applying a fixed-sample tail bound at the random count T_i(t).

The unbounded 1-subgaussian rewards are not covered by the repository's bounded-variable Hoeffding/Azuma interfaces. ML-68 therefore removes those as suppliers and uses only exact independent-random-element/product-law, nonnegative integration, Markov, and exponential-order interfaces.

Defines independence of a finite family of measurable random elements through independence of their generated sigma-algebras.
For a finite independent family, the joint law is the finite product of marginal laws; applies to the finite reward table indexed by (s,i).
Defines nonnegative extended expectation and finite expectation for integrable variables.
For nonnegative measurable Z and a>0, P(Z>=a)<=E[Z]/a; used after exponentiation of a fixed-prefix sum.

For a nonnegative product-measurable integrand on sigma-finite spaces, permits the iterated/product integral equality used to factor MGF integrals under product reward laws. Probability marginals are finite and hence sigma-finite.
Supplies monotonicity and nonnegative scalar homogeneity of the integral.
Supplies finite additivity for sums of nonnegative measurable integrands.
Monotonicity allows a one-sided event for a centered sum to imply the corresponding exponential-threshold event before Markov's inequality.
